Adult Sunday School · Voices of the Fundamentalist Movement

Baptist Voices

Why the preachers who shaped Independent Fundamental Baptist churches in the twentieth century said, plainly, that they were Baptists — and glad of it.

A heritage bought with blood is not worn lightly. These men inherited the same conviction traced through every name in our earlier study — and they said so, in their own words, from their own pulpits.

Jack Hyles
“I am a Baptist. I thank God that I am a Baptist. I thank God for my Baptist heritage. I thank God for Baptist distinctives. I thank God for the men who died for them. If they can be martyred for these Baptist distinctives, the least I can do is believe them.” — Jack Hyles, “What Is a Fundamental Baptist Church?”
Jack Hyles
“I am a Baptist fundamentalist, so I go back to the faith and practice of Baptist churches as founded by Jesus during His earthly ministry!” — Jack Hyles, “Let's Be Baptists!” in Enemies of Soul-Winning
Jack Hyles
“I am a Baptist. I have no animosity towards anybody else. There are saved people in many different groups. I have dear friends who are fine Christian people, yet are not members of Baptist churches. But, I do thank God that I am a Baptist, and I love my Baptist heritage.” — Jack Hyles, The Church
John R. Rice
“I am here in a Baptist church, and I am a Baptist preacher…” — John R. Rice, “The Unvarying God”

Rice consistently identified as a Baptist preacher and evangelist while emphasizing biblical authority and soul-winning over denominational loyalty. He broke with the Southern Baptist Convention and founded independent Baptist ministries and The Sword of the Lord.

Lester Roloff
“And as far as a lot of Baptists are concerned, I guess I'm just a knothole Baptist; I'm on the outside but still seeing and saying what the Lord wants me to say which, when summed up, makes me a premillennial Southern Baptist, especially since I live in Corpus Christi with love for all and malice toward none.” — Lester Roloff, 1956 “Swan Song” address at Baylor University

In the same message, Roloff called for a return to “the old landmarks, namely the sovereignty of the local church, the independence of the pulpit, the authority of the Word of God…”

Closing Thought

Heritage, Held Plainly

None of these men were ashamed of the name. They stood in a line stretching back through every century of this study, and they said so from the pulpit — not out of pride in a denomination, but out of loyalty to a doctrine of the church older than any denomination's name.
